scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor configuration review
scenarios.situation: Reviewing a Start Here: Ground Floor configuration before production. Something looks off.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important misconfiguration to check?
choices: Security settings: overly permissive access is the most common and dangerous misconfiguration
Performance tuning: suboptimal but rarely critical at deploy
Naming conventions: annoying but not dangerous
Documentation: a problem but not a deployment blocker
scenarios.why: Security misconfigurations create immediate vulnerability. Verify auth, authz, encryption first. In MongoDB, working-but-insecure is worse than delayed-but-secure.
scenarios.hint: What causes the most damage if wrong?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor performance issue
scenarios.situation: Users report Start Here: Ground Floor is slow. It was fast last week. No config changes made.
choices: Check resource utilization and data/traffic growth: regressions without config changes mean resource exhaustion or growth
Restart all services
Increase timeouts
Roll back to last week's backup
scenarios.why: Without config changes, causes are resource pressure or data growth. Check metrics first. Restarting masks problems; timeouts treat symptoms.
scenarios.hint: If config did not change, what did?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor failure diagnosis
scenarios.situation: A critical Start Here: Ground Floor component failed. Diagnose quickly to restore service.
choices: Reproduce and scope, check logs/metrics, isolate the layer, hypothesize, test fix, verify
Try the most common fix first
Restart everything
Call for help immediately
scenarios.why: Systematic order preserves evidence and avoids wasted effort. Skipping to common fixes fails on uncommon issues; restarts destroy diagnostics.
scenarios.hint: Which approach preserves evidence?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor design decision
scenarios.situation: Designing new Start Here: Ground Floor: simple (current needs) vs comprehensive (future scale).
choices: Start simple with clear extension points; avoid both under- and over-engineering
Always comprehensive: future-proof everything
Always simple: YAGNI
Team vote
scenarios.why: Balance current needs with likely evolution. Ask: what is the cost of being wrong in each direction?
scenarios.hint: What balances the extremes?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor security incident
scenarios.situation: Monitoring shows suspicious Start Here: Ground Floor activity. Might be attack or false positive.
choices: Contain first (isolate, preserve evidence), then investigate in parallel
Investigate fully before acting
Shut everything down
Ignore if service is normal
scenarios.why: Contain to prevent spread while preserving forensics (isolate network, do not power off). Shutdowns destroy evidence; ignoring alerts breeds breaches.
scenarios.hint: How to balance stopping threat vs preserving evidence?

scenarios.title: Start Here: Ground Floor scaling challenge
scenarios.situation: Start Here: Ground Floor must handle 10x traffic next quarter.
choices: Measure bottlenecks, scale the constrained resource; verify, repeat
Scale everything 10x now
Rewrite for new scale
Add caching everywhere
scenarios.why: Data-driven targeted scaling: load test, find bottlenecks, scale specifically, verify next constraint. Uniform scaling wastes resources; rewrites are risky.
scenarios.hint: Why targeted over uniform scaling?

choices: Embed — order line items are always read with the order, never shared, and bounded in count; one read returns everything, no joins
Reference — embedding is never correct
Embed the customer document inside every order too
Store line items in a separate database
scenarios.hint: Are line items ever queried without their order?
scenarios.prompt: Embed or reference the line items, and what rule decides?
scenarios.situation: Orders with line items. The app always shows items with the order; items are never queried standalone and number in the dozens.
scenarios.title: The order document
scenarios.why: Schema design follows access patterns: data accessed together should live together. Line items are bounded, exclusively owned by the order, and always read with it — embedding gives single-read retrieval with no $lookup. Reference when: the related data is unbounded (comments on a viral post), shared across parents, or queried independently. The 16 MB document limit is the hard ceiling on embedding.

choices: Reference with an array of ObjectIds (or a join collection for rich relationships) — unbounded growth would blow the 16 MB limit and make every read drag the whole history
Embed all 50k readings — reads are simpler
Embed and rely on the 16 MB limit as a warning
Store readings as separate databases per sensor
scenarios.hint: What happens to the document when the array grows by 1,000 entries a day, forever?
scenarios.situation: IoT sensors emit readings every minute. A developer embeds all readings in the sensor document — 50k entries and growing.
scenarios.title: The growing sensor
scenarios.why: Unbounded arrays are the classic embedding failure: the document grows forever toward the 16 MB limit, every read/write drags the whole history, and updates rewrite a giant document. Pattern: reference — readings in their own collection with sensor_id (bucket pattern for time series: one document per sensor per hour). Embed only bounded, co-accessed data.

choices: Subset pattern — embed the frequently-accessed fields (name, price) and reference the full document; or extended reference with the fields queries need
Always embed the entire product document
Denormalization is never acceptable
Duplicate the whole product on every read via $lookup
scenarios.hint: Which fields does the order history page actually display?
scenarios.prompt: How do you avoid a $lookup per order without duplicating everything?
scenarios.situation: Order history shows product name + price per line. $lookup per order is slow; embedding full product docs duplicates megabytes.
scenarios.title: The product name problem
scenarios.why: The subset/extended-reference pattern: duplicate only the fields the access pattern needs (name, price at purchase time — which is also historically correct, since prices change) and keep a reference id for the rest. Denormalization is a deliberate, bounded trade: faster reads, stale-copy risk on updates. For order history, the snapshot is a feature — the price at purchase must not change.

choices: Schema validation with $jsonSchema — enforce required fields and types at the database level; flexible schema doesn't mean no schema
Validation is impossible in MongoDB
Enforce schema only in application code — the database can't help
Require all documents to have identical fields
scenarios.hint: Flexible schema means the database doesn't force one — but can you opt into enforcement?
scenarios.prompt: How do you enforce data quality without losing flexibility?
scenarios.situation: A users collection has email as string, number, missing, and nested object across documents. Queries break unpredictably.
scenarios.title: The wild-west collection
scenarios.why: MongoDB's flexible schema is opt-out of rigidity, not opt-out of discipline: $jsonSchema validation rules enforce required fields, types, and patterns at write time (strict or moderate validation levels). 'Schemaless' works for exploration; production collections need validation — the database should reject bad writes, not just the app.

choices: Polymorphic pattern — one collection with a type discriminator field; queries filter by type, indexes include the discriminator
Separate database per subtype
One collection per subtype always
Store the type in the collection name
scenarios.hint: How do you keep 'all notifications' queryable together while distinguishing email from SMS?
scenarios.prompt: How do you model subtypes in one collection?
scenarios.situation: Notifications: email (subject, body), SMS (phone, text), push (device token). The app lists 'all notifications for user X' and also per-type views.
scenarios.title: The notification subtypes
scenarios.why: The polymorphic pattern: single collection, a type field (e.g., kind: 'email'|'sms'|'push'), each subtype carrying its own fields. One query serves the unified timeline; type-filtered queries + discriminator in indexes serve per-type views. Separate collections would make 'all notifications sorted by time' expensive. The discriminator is the key to indexing and querying sanity.

choices: Attribute pattern — convert varying attributes to an array of {k, v} pairs; index 'attrs.k' and 'attrs.v' once instead of per-attribute indexes
Create one index per attribute — indexes are free
Store attributes as separate collections
Dynamic keys are fine; queries handle them
scenarios.hint: If attribute names are data (not schema), how do you index 'all possible attribute names'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you model products with wildly varying attributes?
scenarios.situation: A catalog has products with 5 to 200 varying attributes (color, voltage, thread-count...). Dynamic field names make indexing impossible.
scenarios.title: The 200-attribute product
scenarios.why: The attribute pattern turns dynamic keys into data: an array of {k, v} sub-documents. Now one compound index on (attrs.k, attrs.v) serves queries on any attribute, and queries use dot notation into the array. Dynamic top-level field names are an anti-pattern — they defeat indexing, validation, and query planning.

choices: $set — updates only the named fields; a replacement-style update (no operators) overwrites the whole document, deleting fields you didn't mention
They are identical; $set is just verbose
Replacement updates merge fields automatically
$set deletes unspecified fields
scenarios.hint: What happens to 'role' if you update without $set?
scenarios.prompt: What does $set do that a bare update document doesn't?
scenarios.situation: A developer 'updates' a user with {name: 'Ada', level: 6} (no operators) and the role field vanishes.
scenarios.title: The vanishing field
scenarios.why: An update document without operators is a replacement: the entire document becomes exactly what you passed — unspecified fields are deleted. $set (and friends: $inc, $push, $unset) modify only named paths, leaving the rest intact. Rule: use update operators for partial changes; use replacement only when you mean 'this document is now exactly this'.

choices: Upsert (update with upsert:true) — atomically inserts when no document matches, updates when one does; the filter + update define the resulting document
Find-then-insert in application code — the gap is harmless
insertOne and catch duplicate key errors — cleaner semantics
Upserts can't set fields on insert
scenarios.hint: What happens between your find and your insert when two processes run concurrently?
scenarios.situation: A sequence counter: read current value, increment, write back. Under concurrency, two processes read the same value and duplicate sequence numbers.
scenarios.title: The race on the counter
scenarios.why: Upsert makes find-and-modify atomic: one operation either updates the match or inserts. $setOnInsert sets fields only on the insert path (created timestamp), while $inc applies either way. The find-then-insert pattern has a race window; upsert closes it. It's the standard atomic counter / get-or-create idiom.

choices: $push appends to an array (with $each/$slice/$sort modifiers); $addToSet appends only if absent — use $addToSet for set semantics
$push and $addToSet are identical
Use $set with the whole array — simplest
Arrays can't be updated atomically
scenarios.hint: Which one dedupes, and which modifiers bound the array size?
scenarios.prompt: How do $push and $addToSet differ, and how do you cap array growth?
scenarios.situation: Tags must stay unique per user; a comments array must keep only the latest 10.
scenarios.title: The array operators
scenarios.why: $push appends (allowing duplicates); $addToSet appends only absent values (set semantics). $push modifiers: $each (multiple), $slice (keep last N — bounds growth), $sort (ordered insert), $position. The $slice: -10 pattern is how you keep 'latest N' arrays from growing unbounded — combining with the schema lesson on unbounded arrays.

choices: deleteMany({}) with no filter deletes everything — always filter explicitly, and prefer deleteOne when one document is intended; bulk writes need ordered:false consideration
deleteMany requires a filter; empty filter errors
Deletes are always safe; there's a recycle bin
deleteOne deletes all matches
scenarios.hint: What does 'deleteMany with an empty filter' match?
scenarios.prompt: What is the dangerous delete pattern?
scenarios.situation: A cleanup script meant to delete expired sessions runs db.sessions.deleteMany({}) — wiping all sessions, active ones included.
scenarios.title: The empty filter
scenarios.why: An empty filter matches everything — deleteMany({}) is 'delete all'. Discipline: always write the filter first, test it with find()/countDocuments(), then delete; use deleteOne when exactly one document is intended. For bulk operations, ordered:false continues past individual failures. Destructive ops deserve a read-before-write habit.

choices: The positional $ operator updates the first matching array element; arrayFilters update specific elements by condition — $[elem] with arrayFilters for multi-element conditional updates
Positional $ updates all matches
Array elements can't be updated in place
Rewrite the whole array with $set
scenarios.hint: $ = first match; $[identifier] + arrayFilters = conditional matches. Which do you need?
scenarios.prompt: How do you update elements inside an array?
scenarios.situation: Increment qty for SKU 'A1' in an order's items array; separately, mark all items with qty > 10 as backordered.
scenarios.title: The nested update
scenarios.why: The positional $ operator addresses the first array element matching the query filter — good for single-element updates. For conditional multi-element updates, filtered positional $[id] with arrayFilters selects elements by predicate. Without these, you'd read-modify-write the whole array (race-prone). Know both: $ for first match, arrayFilters for many.

choices: findOneAndUpdate — atomically finds, modifies, and returns the document (before or after); the read-modify-write race disappears
find then update — the window is microseconds, harmless
Updates can't return the document
Use $setOnInsert for this
scenarios.hint: Which operation claims the job and tells you which job you claimed, atomically?
scenarios.prompt: What is the atomic job-queue claim pattern?
scenarios.situation: Workers claim queued jobs. Find-then-update lets two workers claim the same job.
scenarios.title: The job queue race
scenarios.why: findOneAndUpdate is atomic: it matches, modifies, and returns the document in one step — the claim and the read can't interleave with another worker. Options: sort (highest priority first), returnDocument before/after, upsert. It's the standard primitive for queues, locks, and counters in MongoDB.

choices: $match early — filter before $group/$lookup so later stages process fewer documents; indexes serve $match only at the pipeline start
$group first — grouping reduces data, so it should lead
Stage order doesn't affect performance
$match last — filter the final results
scenarios.hint: Which stage can use an index — and only in which position?
scenarios.situation: A pipeline groups 10M orders then matches the year. It times out; moving $match first fixes it.
scenarios.title: The pipeline order
scenarios.why: $match at the pipeline start can use indexes and shrinks the working set for every downstream stage ($group, $sort, $lookup). Late $match processes the full 10M through expensive stages first. Rule: filter early, shape late. (The optimizer coalesces adjacent $matches, but don't rely on it — write it right.)

choices: $unwind deconstructs the array into one document per element; preserveNullAndEmptyArrays:true keeps documents with missing/empty arrays (like a LEFT JOIN)
$unwind deletes documents with empty arrays by design — unavoidable
Use $group instead of $unwind
Arrays can't be unwound if empty
scenarios.hint: What happens to a document whose array is empty — does it survive $unwind?
scenarios.prompt: What does $unwind do, and how do you keep empty-array documents?
scenarios.situation: Counting line items per order drops orders with no items entirely.
scenarios.title: The disappearing orders
scenarios.why: $unwind emits one document per array element — documents with missing/empty arrays vanish by default (inner-join semantics). preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true keeps them with the field as null/missing (left-join semantics). Choose deliberately: dropping empties is right for 'average items per order with items'; keeping them is right for 'orders including empty ones'.

choices: $lookup — left-outer-join equivalent pulling customer docs into an array; then $unwind if one-to-one is expected
$lookup is an inner join
Joins are impossible in aggregation
Embed instead — $lookup is never the answer
scenarios.hint: What does the 'as' array contain when there's no match?
scenarios.prompt: How do you join collections, and what are the semantics?
scenarios.situation: Orders need customer names. The team debates $lookup vs denormalization.
scenarios.title: The order-customer join
scenarios.why: $lookup performs a left outer join: matching docs land in the 'as' array (empty array when no match — hence the $unwind to flatten one-to-one). It's correct but costs a per-document lookup — fine at moderate scale, painful at huge scale or high QPS. That's the denormalization trade again: $lookup for correctness/flexibility, embedding for hot paths.

choices: $group with _id as the key and accumulators ($sum, $avg, $push) — _id: null groups everything into one row; $project then shapes the output
$group can't compute multiple accumulators
_id is always the document _id
Grouping requires a $sort first
scenarios.hint: What does _id mean inside $group — the document's _id, or the group key?
scenarios.prompt: How does $group work, and what is _id inside it?
scenarios.situation: Regional quarterly totals with averages and counts. A developer sets _id: '$_id' and gets per-document groups.
scenarios.title: The grouping key
scenarios.why: In $group, _id is the group key (not the document id): _id: '$region' groups by region; _id: {r:'$region', q:'$quarter'} makes composite keys; _id: null collapses everything to one group. Accumulators ($sum/$avg/$min/$max/$push/$addToSet) compute per group. $project after $group renames _id into readable fields.

choices: $facet — multiple sub-pipelines over the same input in one pass (e.g., by-status counts + top products + histogram) for dashboards
Run three separate aggregations — simpler
$facet runs pipelines sequentially — no benefit
Facets can't share the input
scenarios.hint: How do you compute three different breakdowns of the same filtered set in one database round trip?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard needs: orders by status, top 5 products, and a value histogram — all for 2026. Three round trips today.
scenarios.title: The dashboard query
scenarios.why: $facet runs multiple sub-pipelines against the same input documents in a single aggregation — one $match, then parallel facets. One round trip, consistent snapshot across all breakdowns. Watch memory: each facet buffers its results (100 MB stage limit applies unless allowDiskUse). For dashboards, $facet is the standard.

choices: $bucket/$bucketAuto — group numeric values into ranges (histograms); $bucketAuto distributes evenly by count, $bucket needs explicit boundaries
$group can't do ranges
Histogram requires application code
$bucketAuto uses fixed boundaries
scenarios.hint: Which stage maps a continuous value into labeled buckets?
scenarios.prompt: How do you build a value histogram in the pipeline?
scenarios.title: The histogram
scenarios.why: $bucket groups by computed ranges: boundaries define the bins, default catches outliers, output accumulates per bin. $bucketAuto instead takes a bucket count and sizes bins for even document distribution. Both beat fetching all values and histogramming in app code — the database does the counting.

choices: ESR rule — Equality, Sort, Range: index {status: 1, created: -1, amount: 1} serves equality on status, sort on created, range on amount; order matters
Index field order doesn't matter
Put the range field first for selectivity
Single-field indexes are always better
scenarios.hint: Equality first, then sort, then range — what order do the index keys go in?
scenarios.prompt: How do you order fields in a compound index for this query?
scenarios.situation: A frequent query filters status (equality), amount (range), sorts by created. The current index {amount: 1, status: 1} isn't used well.
scenarios.title: The compound index
scenarios.why: ESR (Equality, Sort, Range): equality fields first (they narrow to exact key ranges), then sort fields (avoids in-memory sort), then range fields last (a range scan can't efficiently continue to later fields). {status: 1, created: -1, amount: 1} serves filter + sort + range. Prefix rule: the index also serves queries using just {status} or {status, created} — but not {amount} alone.

choices: explain('executionStats') — check winning plan: IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, nReturned vs totalDocsExamined, and whether the sort was in-memory
The query returns fast, so it's fine
explain() only shows the estimated plan
Keys examined doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN — which one proves the index was used?
scenarios.prompt: How do you verify index usage?
scenarios.situation: An index exists but the query is still slow. The team assumes the index is being used.
scenarios.title: The unused index
scenarios.why: explain('executionStats') shows the winning plan and real stats: stage IXSCAN = index used, COLLSCAN = full collection scan (the smoking gun). Compare totalDocsExamined vs nReturned — examining 1M docs to return 10 means the index isn't selective or isn't used. Also check for in-memory sorts (no index on sort field). Never assume; explain.

choices: TTL index on createdAt (expireAfterSeconds) — MongoDB auto-deletes expired docs; it's for expiry, not archiving — pair with a change stream if you need the data elsewhere
TTL indexes archive data to cold storage
A cron job deleting manually is the only way
TTL works on any field type
scenarios.hint: What does the TTL monitor actually do to expired documents?
scenarios.prompt: How do you auto-expire sessions, and what is the caveat?
scenarios.situation: Sessions must vanish 1 hour after creation. A cron job deletes them hourly, with gaps and load spikes.
scenarios.title: The session expiry
scenarios.why: A TTL index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds auto-removes documents via a background thread (~60s granularity). Caveats: deletion is a delete (data is gone — TTL is not archival; use change streams to copy data out first if needed), and it requires a BSON date field (not a string timestamp). Replace cron deletes with TTL for steady-state expiry.

choices: Partial index with partialFilterExpression — indexes only docs matching the filter (e.g., active users), smaller and faster; sparse indexes are the legacy variant
Index everything; partial indexes are slower
Sparse and partial are identical
Partial indexes can't be unique
scenarios.hint: Why index 10M archived users when queries only touch 100k active ones?
scenarios.prompt: How do you index a subset of documents?
scenarios.situation: Queries filter active users by email; 99% of users are archived. A full unique index on email is huge and slow to build.
scenarios.title: The partial index
scenarios.why: Partial indexes (partialFilterExpression) index only matching documents — smaller, faster builds, less write overhead. They can be unique (uniqueness enforced within the subset). Sparse indexes (legacy) index only docs having the field. Rule: if queries always include the filter predicate, a partial index is strictly better than a full one.

choices: Text index (one per collection) for language-aware search with weights; Atlas Search for real relevance/facets — text indexes are not a search engine
Text indexes rank by relevance like Elasticsearch
Multiple text indexes per collection are fine
Regex on an indexed field is equivalent
scenarios.hint: When does 'search' need stemming and relevance scoring versus just matching?
scenarios.prompt: What are the text-search options, and their limits?
scenarios.situation: Product search needs 'blue shirt' to match 'blue shirts' with relevance ranking. LIKE-style regex is slow and dumb.
scenarios.title: The search box
scenarios.why: A text index enables $text queries: stemming ('shirts'→'shirt'), stop words, per-field weights, one per collection. It's basic relevance — not faceting, not typo tolerance. For real search (fuzzy, autocomplete, facets), Atlas Search (Lucene-based) is the answer. Regex scans can't use indexes efficiently for leading wildcards. Match the tool to the search quality bar.

choices: Write amplification — each index is maintained on every insert/update/delete; index only what queries need, drop unused (check $indexStats)
Indexes never slow writes measurably
More indexes always help reads enough to offset
Write concern affects index maintenance
scenarios.hint: A document insert with 8 indexes — how many index writes happen?
scenarios.prompt: What is the cost of over-indexing?
scenarios.situation: A write-heavy events collection has 8 indexes 'just in case'. Write throughput is half of expected.
scenarios.title: The index tax
scenarios.why: Every index costs on every write: 8 indexes ≈ 8 index maintenance writes per document insert, plus bigger working set and slower builds. $indexStats (ops since server restart) identifies unused indexes — drop them. Index for the queries you have (verified with explain), not the queries you imagine.

choices: Majority of voting members must agree — with 3 nodes, 2 must be up; the partitioned single node steps down (no majority) and the 2-node side elects a primary
The single node stays primary — it was primary first
Both sides elect primaries — split brain is fine
Elections require all members reachable
scenarios.hint: How many votes make a majority of 3? Can the isolated node reach that alone?
scenarios.prompt: What happens in a network partition, and why is there no split brain?
scenarios.situation: A 3-node replica set splits: primary isolated alone, two secondaries together. Both sides think the other is dead.
scenarios.title: The partition
scenarios.why: Elections need a strict majority of voting members (2 of 3). The lone primary can't reach majority → steps down to secondary. The pair elects one of themselves primary. Majority rule is what prevents split brain — the minority side can never elect. (This is why even node counts are discouraged: 2 nodes need both up for majority — no fault tolerance.)

choices: Write concern majority — acknowledged after a majority of voting members apply it (durable through a primary failure); w:1 is faster but can roll back
w:1 is the safest
Write concern controls read speed
Majority means all nodes
scenarios.hint: If the primary acknowledges and then dies before replicating, what happens to your write?
scenarios.prompt: What durability does each write concern buy?
scenarios.situation: A payment write is acknowledged, the primary crashes a second later, and the write is gone — rolled back on the new primary.
scenarios.title: The vanished payment
scenarios.why: w:1 acknowledges when the primary applies the write — if it dies before replicating, the write rolls back. w:'majority' waits until a majority of voting members have it — it survives any single-node failure. Journaling (j:true) adds crash durability on the node. Rule: payments/ledgers → majority; metrics/logs → w:1 is fine. Durability is a dial, not a default.

choices: High-cardinality, evenly-distributed, query-aligned key (e.g., hashed user_id) — spreads writes and chunks evenly; monotonic keys (ObjectId/timestamp) create hot shards
Monotonic ObjectId — it's unique, so it's perfect
Low-cardinality status field — few chunks, simple
Shard key can be changed anytime cheaply
scenarios.hint: If every new document lands on the 'max' chunk, which shard gets all the writes?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a good shard key, and what is the hot-shard failure?
scenarios.situation: A time-series collection sharded on timestamp: one shard holds 80% of data and all writes; others idle.
scenarios.title: The hot shard
scenarios.why: Monotonically increasing shard keys (timestamps, ObjectIds) route all new writes to the max chunk's shard — a hotspot that defeats sharding. Good keys: high cardinality (many distinct values → many chunks), even distribution, and aligned with query patterns (queries including the shard key target one shard). Hashed sharding fixes distribution but scatters range queries. Shard key choice is the most consequential sharding decision — changing it later is expensive.

choices: Oplog — the capped collection recording all writes; secondaries tail it to replicate. Lag = secondary's optime behind primary's; monitor replication lag, size the oplog for the maintenance window
The oplog is optional
Lag is measured in documents, not time
Secondaries read datafiles directly
scenarios.hint: What ordered log do secondaries follow, and what happens if a secondary falls behind past the log's window?
scenarios.prompt: How does replication work, and what bounds it?
scenarios.situation: A secondary was down for 2 days; on return it needs a full resync — the oplog window was only 24h.
scenarios.title: The stale secondary
scenarios.why: The oplog is a capped collection of all writes; secondaries tail it asynchronously. If a secondary lags beyond the oplog window, it can't catch up incrementally → needs full resync. Size the oplog to cover expected downtimes (maintenance windows + margin). Monitor replication lag (optimeDate gap) — growing lag is the early warning.

choices: Read preference + maxStaleness — primary (default, consistent), secondary (offload, possibly stale), nearest (lowest latency); set maxStalenessSeconds to bound staleness
Read preference changes write routing
Secondary reads are always consistent
Nearest always reads from the primary
scenarios.hint: Which setting says 'I'll read from a secondary, but never one more than 90 seconds stale'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you offload reads without reading ancient data?
scenarios.situation: Analytics queries hammer the primary. The team wants secondary reads but fears stale data.
scenarios.title: The read offload
scenarios.why: Read preferences route reads: primary (default, strongly consistent), primaryPreferred, secondary, secondaryPreferred, nearest (latency-based). Secondary reads may be stale (replication lag) — maxStalenessSeconds caps how stale a secondary can be to serve reads. Analytics → secondaryPreferred + maxStaleness; money → primary. It's a consistency/latency dial per operation.

choices: Arbiter — votes in elections but holds no data; used to make an even node count odd cheaply (but provides no data redundancy)

Two arbiters are better than one

choices: mongodump/mongorestore for logical backup (portable, selective); filesystem/LVM snapshots for large deployments (fast, consistent with journaling); test restores regularly — method depends on size and RTO
mongodump is the only backup method
Snapshots are inconsistent by nature
Backups don't need testing

Application users need dbAdmin

choices: Balancer migrates chunks between shards to even out distribution; it runs in a window you configure — monitor balancer state and chunk distribution during/after key changes
The balancer is always on and instant
Chunk migration requires downtime
Balancing is manual only

choices: mongostat/mongotop + serverStatus metrics (opcounters, connections, queues, replication lag) → feed to real monitoring (Prometheus/Atlas); alert on queues, page faults/cache pressure, replication lag
Logs alone are sufficient monitoring
Monitoring is optional for small deployments

choices: Feature compatibility version (FCV) gates new features; upgrade binaries then setFCV forward — and you can downgrade by setting FCV back (within limits); always test on staging
Upgrades are in-place with no steps
FCV is cosmetic
Downgrades are impossible

choices: Profiler (database profiler levels 0/1/2) + system.profile collection; or Atlas Performance Advisor; enable selectively — level 2 logs everything and costs I/O
The profiler is always on by default
Slow queries can't be captured
Profiling has zero overhead

scenarios.title: The Documents & Schema Mystery

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Documents & Schema?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Documents & Schema issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Documents & Schema is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

This method works for any Documents & Schema failure in Mongodb.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Documents & Schema
evidence: All Documents & Schema components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

lessons.title: Documents & Schema — Core concepts
concepts: Embedding vs referencing: unbounded arrays are the classic embedding failure: the document grows forever toward the 16 MB limit, every read/write drags the whole history, and updates rewrite a giant document.

Access patterns: schema design follows access patterns: data accessed together should live together. MongoDB's flexible schema is opt-out of rigidity, not opt-out of discipline: $jsonSchema validation rules enforce required fields, types, and patterns at write time (strict or moderate validation levels).
Unbounded arrays: reference when: the related data is unbounded (comments on a viral post), shared across parents, or queried independently.
16MB limit: the 16 MB document limit is the hard ceiling on embedding.
Denormalization is a deliberate, bounded trade: faster reads, stale-copy risk on updates.

Subset pattern: the subset/extended-reference pattern: duplicate only the fields the access pattern needs (name, price at purchase time — which is also historically correct, since prices change) and keep a reference id for the rest.

example.walkthrough: MongoDB's flexible schema is opt-out of rigidity, not opt-out of discipline: $jsonSchema validation rules enforce required fields, types, and patterns at write time (strict or moderate validation levels). 'Schemaless' works for exploration; production collections need validation — the database should reject bad writes, not just the app.

pitfalls: Common trap: require all documents to have identical fields.
Common trap: dynamic keys are fine; queries handle them.
Common trap: embed and rely on the 16 MB limit as a warning.
Common trap: enforce schema only in application code.

lessons.title: CRUD — Core concepts
concepts: Update operators: rule: use update operators for partial changes; use replacement only when you mean 'this document is now exactly this'.

$set: an update document without operators is a replacement: the entire document becomes exactly what you passed — unspecified fields are deleted. $set (and friends: $inc, $push, $unset) modify only named paths, leaving the rest intact.
Upsert: the find-then-insert pattern has a race window; upsert closes it. Options: sort (highest priority first), returnDocument before/after, upsert.
Array update operators: the positional $ operator addresses the first array element matching the query filter — good for single-element updates.

example.code:
db.users.updateOne({_id: 1}, {$addToSet: {tags: "vip"}});
db.posts.updateOne({_id: 9}, {$push: {comments: {$each: [c1, c2], $slice: -10}}})
example.walkthrough: $push appends (allowing duplicates); $addToSet appends only absent values (set semantics). $push modifiers: $each (multiple), $slice (keep last N — bounds growth), $sort (ordered insert), $position. The $slice: -10 pattern is how you keep 'latest N' arrays from growing unbounded — combining with the schema lesson on unbounded arrays.

pitfalls: Common trap: use $set with the whole array.
Common trap: upserts can't set fields on insert.
Common trap: array elements can't be updated in place.

lessons.title: Aggregation — Core concepts
concepts: Pipeline optimization: $match at the pipeline start can use indexes and shrinks the working set for every downstream stage ($group, $sort, $lookup).

$match placement: $lookup performs a left outer join: matching docs land in the 'as' array (empty array when no match — hence the $unwind to flatten one-to-one). $facet runs multiple sub-pipelines against the same input documents in a single aggregation — one $match, then parallel facets.

$unwind emits one document per array element — documents with missing/empty arrays vanish by default (inner-join semantics). preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true keeps them with the field as null/missing (left-join semantics).
$lookup: that's the denormalization trade again: $lookup for correctness/flexibility, embedding for hot paths.

example.code:
db.orders.aggregate([
  {$unwind: {path: "$items", preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true}},
  {$group: {_id: "$_id", count: {$sum: 1}}}])
example.walkthrough: $unwind emits one document per array element — documents with missing/empty arrays vanish by default (inner-join semantics). preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true keeps them with the field as null/missing (left-join semantics). Choose deliberately: dropping empties is right for 'average items per order with items'; keeping them is right for 'orders including empty ones'.

pitfalls: Common trap: $group can't compute multiple accumulators.
Common trap: $unwind deletes documents with empty arrays by design.

lessons.title: Indexes — Core concepts
concepts: Compound indexes: partial indexes (partialFilterExpression) index only matching documents — smaller, faster builds, less write overhead.

ESR rule: rule: if queries always include the filter predicate, a partial index is strictly better than a full one. Prefix rule: the index also serves queries using just {status} or {status, created} — but not {amount} alone.

explain(): explain('executionStats') shows the winning plan and real stats: stage IXSCAN = index used, COLLSCAN = full collection scan (the smoking gun). Index for the queries you have (verified with explain), not the queries you imagine.
TTL indexes: sparse indexes (legacy) index only docs having the field. A TTL index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds auto-removes documents via a background thread (~60s granularity).
Partial indexes: regex scans can't use indexes efficiently for leading wildcards.

example.code:
db.users.createIndex({email: 1},
 {unique: true, partialFilterExpression: {status: "active"}})
example.walkthrough: Partial indexes (partialFilterExpression) index only matching documents — smaller, faster builds, less write overhead. They can be unique (uniqueness enforced within the subset).

pitfalls: Common trap: index everything; partial indexes are slower.
Common trap: TTL indexes archive data to cold storage.
Common trap: text indexes rank by relevance like Elasticsearch.
Common trap: multiple text indexes per collection are fine.

lessons.title: Replication & Sharding — Core concepts
concepts: Replica set elections: elections need a strict majority of voting members (2 of 3). An arbiter is a voting-only member: no data, minimal resources, exists to give an odd vote count so elections can reach majority.

Majority: w:1 acknowledges when the primary applies the write — if it dies before replicating, the write rolls back. w:'majority' waits until a majority of voting members have it — it survives any single-node failure.
Durability: journaling (j:true) adds crash durability on the node.
Shard key choice is the most consequential sharding decision — changing it later is expensive.
Oplog: the oplog is a capped collection of all writes; secondaries tail it asynchronously.

lessons.title: MongoDB — Core concepts
concepts: Model for the read path: embed data that is accessed together (comments with posts), reference data that is shared or unbounded — and never let an array grow without a bound.
The 16 MB document limit is a design constraint, not a suggestion. Unbounded arrays (event histories, logs) belong in the bucket pattern: one document per entity per time window.
The aggregation pipeline is a chain of stages — $match and $project early to shrink the working set, $unwind to flatten arrays before $group, and remember each stage's 100 MB memory limit.
Index for your queries, then verify with explain(): COLLSCAN means a full scan, IXSCAN means the index is working, and docsExamined should be close to nReturned.
Write concern is a durability contract: w:1 means 'the primary has it', w:'majority' means 'it survives a failover'. Choose per write based on what losing it would cost.
Replica sets give high availability, not magic. Failover is fast but not instant; design clients to retry with idempotent writes and read with a concern that matches your consistency needs.

example.code:
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "shipped" } },
  { $unwind: "$lineItems" },
  { $group: { _id: "$lineItems.productId",
              revenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$lineItems.qty", "$lineItems.price"] } } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])
example.walkthrough: $match first so only shipped orders flow downstream; $unwind flattens each order's lineItems into per-item documents; $group sums revenue per product; $sort/$limit take the top 10 — filtering early keeps the heavy $group stage small.

pitfalls: Common trap: embedding unbounded arrays — documents bloat toward 16 MB and updates rewrite megabytes; use the bucket pattern.
Common trap: $group directly on documents containing arrays — it aggregates documents, not array elements; $unwind first.
Common trap: trusting default w:1 for critical writes — acknowledged does not mean replicated; use w:'majority' where loss is unacceptable.
Common trap: reading explain() output as 'it used an index, so it's fast' — check docsExamined vs nReturned; an index scan over millions of keys is still slow.

labs.title: Embedding vs referencing — mongosh drill
labs.objective: Run a short sequence of mongosh commands that demonstrates embedding vs referencing, then verify each result against the expected output.
steps: This lab reworks the Documents & Schema practice scenario "The order document" into commands you run yourself — same concept, hands-on instead of multiple choice.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: show dbs — the database list includes admin
Type exactly: db.users.find() — the documents carry the name field
Type exactly: db.users.insertOne({name: "lab"}) — the write result is acknowledged
In your own words, say what each command's output taught you about embedding vs referencing.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `show dbs`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "admin".

sections.heading: Documents & Schema
items: Embedding vs referencing — unbounded arrays are the classic embedding failure: the document grows forever toward the 16 MB limit, every read/write drags the whole history, and updates rewrite a giant document.

Access patterns — schema design follows access patterns: data accessed together should live together. MongoDB's flexible schema is opt-out of rigidity, not opt-out of discipline: $jsonSchema validation rules enforce required fields, types, and patterns at write time (strict…
Unbounded arrays — reference when: the related data is unbounded (comments on a viral post), shared across parents, or queried independently.
16MB limit — the 16 MB document limit is the hard ceiling on embedding.
Denormalization is a deliberate, bounded trade — faster reads, stale-copy risk on updates.

Subset pattern — the subset/extended-reference pattern: duplicate only the fields the access pattern needs (name, price at purchase time — which is also historically correct, since prices change) and keep a reference id for the rest.
Common trap — require all documents to have identical fields.
Common trap — dynamic keys are fine; queries handle them.
Common trap — embed and rely on the 16 MB limit as a warning.
Common trap — enforce schema only in application code.

sections.heading: CRUD
items: Update operators — rule: use update operators for partial changes; use replacement only when you mean 'this document is now exactly this'.
Upsert — the find-then-insert pattern has a race window; upsert closes it. Options: sort (highest priority first), returnDocument before/after, upsert.
Array update operators — the positional $ operator addresses the first array element matching the query filter — good for single-element updates.
Common trap — use $set with the whole array.
Common trap — $set deletes unspecified fields.
Common trap — upserts can't set fields on insert.
Common trap — array elements can't be updated in place.

sections.heading: Aggregation
items: Pipeline optimization — $match at the pipeline start can use indexes and shrinks the working set for every downstream stage ($group, $sort, $lookup).
Common trap — use $group instead of $unwind.
Common trap — $group can't compute multiple accumulators.
Common trap — $unwind deletes documents with empty arrays by design.
Common trap — $facet runs pipelines sequentially.

sections.heading: Indexes
items: Compound indexes — partial indexes (partialFilterExpression) index only matching documents — smaller, faster builds, less write overhead.

ESR rule — rule: if queries always include the filter predicate, a partial index is strictly better than a full one. Prefix rule: the index also serves queries using just {status} or {status, created} — but not {amount} alone.
TTL indexes — sparse indexes (legacy) index only docs having the field. A TTL index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds auto-removes documents via a background thread (~60s granularity).
Partial indexes — regex scans can't use indexes efficiently for leading wildcards.
Common trap — index everything; partial indexes are slower.
Common trap — TTL indexes archive data to cold storage.
Common trap — text indexes rank by relevance like Elasticsearch.
Common trap — multiple text indexes per collection are fine.
Partial — Partial indexes (partialFilterExpression) index only matching documents — smaller, faster builds, less write overhead. They can be unique (uniqueness enforced within the subset).

sections.heading: Replication & Sharding
items: Replica set elections — elections need a strict majority of voting members (2 of 3). An arbiter is a voting-only member: no data, minimal resources, exists to give an odd vote count so elections can reach majority.

Majority — w:1 acknowledges when the primary applies the write — if it dies before replicating, the write rolls back. w:'majority' waits until a majority of voting members have it — it survives any single-node failure.
Durability — journaling (j:true) adds crash durability on the node.
Shard key choice is the most consequential sharding decision — changing it later is expensive.
Oplog — the oplog is a capped collection of all writes; secondaries tail it asynchronously.
Common trap — write concern controls read speed.
Common trap — read preference changes write routing.
Common trap — shard key can be changed anytime cheaply.
Common trap — arbiters are required in every set.

sections.heading: Administration
items: Backup methods — and the iron rule: an untested backup is a hope — restore to a scratch environment on a schedule.
Restore testing — mongodump = logical, portable across versions/topologies, but slow at scale (and restore replays inserts).
RBAC — mongoDB RBAC: grant built-in roles (read, readWrite per database; clusterMonitor for monitoring; dbAdmin for maintenance) or custom roles with specific privileges.
Balancer — check sh.isBalancerRunning()/balancer state, set a balancing window for off-peak, and watch chunk counts per shard converge.
Common trap — chunk migration requires downtime.
Common trap — logs alone are sufficient monitoring.
Common trap — monitoring is optional for small deployments.
Common trap — one admin user for everything.

Elections need a strict majority of voting members (2 of 3). The lone primary can't reach majority → steps down to secondary.

An update document without operators is a replacement: the entire document becomes exactly what you passed — unspecified fields are deleted. $set (and friends: $inc, $push, $unset) modify only named paths, leaving the rest intact.
RBAC: mongoDB RBAC: grant built-in roles (read, readWrite per database; clusterMonitor for monitoring; dbAdmin for maintenance) or custom roles with specific privileges.

MongoDB's flexible schema is opt-out of rigidity, not opt-out of discipline: $jsonSchema validation rules enforce required fields, types, and patterns at write time (strict or moderate validation levels). 'Schemaless' works for explorati…
Partial indexes: regex scans can't use indexes efficiently for leading wildcards.
Shard key choice is the most consequential sharding decision — changing it later is expensive.

The database profiler: level 0 (off), 1 (slow ops > slowms), 2 (all ops) — logged to system.profile (capped collection). Level 1 with a sensible slowms (e.g., 100ms) captures offenders with minimal overhead.
Upsert: the find-then-insert pattern has a race window; upsert closes it. Options: sort (highest priority first), returnDocument before/after, upsert.

Majority: w:1 acknowledges when the primary applies the write — if it dies before replicating, the write rolls back. w:'majority' waits until a majority of voting members have it — it survives any single-node failure.
Unbounded arrays: reference when: the related data is unbounded (comments on a viral post), shared across parents, or queried independently.
Durability: journaling (j:true) adds crash durability on the node.
Denormalization is a deliberate, bounded trade: faster reads, stale-copy risk on updates.

Safe path: upgrade binaries (rolling, secondary-first), verify, then setFeatureCompatibilityVersion to enable new features. FCV is the rollback lever — set it back to downgrade within the supported window.

The attribute pattern turns dynamic keys into data: an array of {k, v} sub-documents. Now one compound index on (attrs.k, attrs.v) serves queries on any attribute, and queries use dot notation into the array.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Documents & Schema: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one CRUD lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Aggregation terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
